heading: Test units: Yon
summary: A Test unit is a source file under server/tests with one Test class. It composes the realm it tests. The compiler writes the context lifecycle and the case driver. ty test invokes it through the same supervisor that serves a route. The controller calls `total`, so it stays public: a call from a test alone does not keep a member public (TY1333).
body:
Select a language tab and copy the files. A test unit is a server/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> file with Test on exactly one class. A test case is any method whose name begins with test. This is a naming rule, not an annotation on each method. A case checks its result with `Assert.equals`, `Assert.isTrue` or `Assert.throws` (JUnit names; Java and Groovy write `Assert.throwsError`, because `throws` is a reserved word there, Go writes `Assert.Equals`, Ruby `Assert.is_true` and PHP `Assert::equals`), and `ValueSource` runs one case for each listed input; see Assert and ValueSource in Test units. Rust has no reflection (a way for code to inspect itself while it runs) that could find an annotated method. Also, a controller route method already starts its name with its verb, which is a similar rule.

Test names the Setup that the context is built from. It also names the partition that the context is built in. UseProfiles and TestSettings go on the same class. They reach the context in the same way as the profiles and properties of a running server. FreshStart is accepted, but its behavior is already the default. The compiler starts a context before every case and disposes of it afterwards. In F#, the case reads it as `this.behaviors`, and the TestSetup declares `static member configure`, as in C#. Run the units with ty test. It runs every unit and reports one line for each case. If any case fails, it exits with a non-zero code at the end.

When a class has an annotation, it needs a test unit. ty preview does not start while any public method of an annotated class was not called by a test* case. Writing the name of the method in a test is not enough, and a call on a Fake does not count. ty test --coverage fails on the same report. Methods that the compiler writes do not need a test. A derived query, a declared HTTP request method and a Convert contain no logic that a person wrote. TAC_ALLOW_UNTESTED=1 lets one run skip the check. ty start never checks.

Fake declares a field that the test assigns. In JavaScript and TypeScript, this.construct(Role) builds the role under test. It uses those fakes (test doubles) in place of its Needs collaborators (the classes that its Needs fields point to). Ruby also gets construct(Role), because Ruby can set a field from outside the class, and Lua gets `self:construct(Role)` (ADR 0085). Java and Groovy get `construct(Role.class)`, Kotlin `construct(Role::class)`, C# `construct<Role>()` and Dart `construct<Role>(Role)`. The role can be a service or a controller: a unit in server/tests can use every controller in server/controllers, SocketRoute controllers and error handlers included, and the error classes in server/errors. It calls a controller method directly, without HTTP. The driver clears every Fake before each case: it becomes null, nil, None or undefined, a number becomes zero and a boolean false. In C# it becomes `default`, and in Go the zero value of its type. A Kotlin or Dart Fake is nullable or has a primitive type, because a `lateinit var` or a `late` field has no empty value and the build refuses it. A Rust case reads the unit through `&self`, so a Rust Fake that a case assigns is a `RefCell` or a `Cell`, and the driver resets it to its `Default`, `None` for an `Option`. F# runs every case on a new instance, so its Fakes start empty too. In F#, a Fake is a settable property, `[<Fake>] member val Names : NameService = Unchecked.defaultof<NameService> with get, set`, and the case builds the role with its Needs properties set: `StockService(Names = this.Names)`. In PHP, a Fake is a typed property with no value, `#[Fake] public CatalogCounterDelegate $catalogCounterDelegate;`. The driver unsets it before every case, and the case passes it to the constructor that Needs gives the role: `new CatalogService($this->catalogCounterDelegate)`. Python, PHP, F#, Go and Rust units have no construct helper (a Go or Rust Tac unit has one), so they pass the Fakes to the role's own constructor or test the logic directly, not through the container. The container is the part of the framework that creates and injects roles.

The test class and its TestSetup live in separate files in the same tests/ folder. The Setup class that Test names, for example Test(CatalogTestSetup), selects the sibling file (the file next to it) by exact class name and source extension. The compiler checks both files that you wrote before it builds the test program. The test configuration is never included in a production browser or server bundle. Tachyon does not load sibling test setups that are not used. You may still select a production Setup yourself instead.

In C++, the unit is `server/tests/CatalogServiceTest.hpp` with one class, `class [[Test(CatalogTestSetup, {"partition":"tests"})]] CatalogServiceTest`. Each public method whose name begins with `test` and that has no parameters is one case. `[[ValueSource([1, 2, 3])]]` on a method with one parameter runs it once for each input, and a case may return `Task<void>`. The TestSetup is `class [[TestSetup]] CatalogTestSetup` in `server/tests/CatalogTestSetup.hpp`. Its static `configure` method returns `BehaviorAdapters`, and you may leave it out. `construct<CatalogService>()` makes a service, a delegate or a controller, and the case calls its methods directly, without HTTP.

A C++ Fake is a field of the test class that holds the stand-in object, such as `[[Fake]] CatalogCounterDelegate catalogCounterDelegate;`. It is not a reference, a pointer or a static field. Its type must be a C++ class of the project in `server/services`, `server/delegates`, `server/converters`, `server/stores`, `server/remotes` or `server/controllers`; otherwise the build stops with `TY1372`. Every case gets a new test object, so each Fake starts as a new object of its class. While `construct<T>()` makes T, every `Needs` field of the Fake's type gets the Fake's object. So the case sets `catalogCounterDelegate.value = 4`, and the service returns 8. A shared object that is first made during `construct` keeps the real objects: the `CatalogService` of the controller still uses the real delegate, so `getTotal` returns 42. A Fake in the TestSetup class is refused. An `[[HTTPClient]]` sends its requests to `adapters.http` of the TestSetup, as in Tac C++ test units.

The field `BehaviorContext behaviors;` receives the context of the case. `[[UseProfiles("test")]]` and `[[TestSettings({"yon.catalog.size":5})]]` give it profiles and properties; the paths in `TestSettings` must start with `yon.`. The markers on the Test class win over the markers on the TestSetup. Each case runs as one invocation: every object is new for each case, OnStart runs when an object is made, events are delivered at the end of the case, and OnStop runs in reverse order when the case ends. `[[FreshStart]]` is accepted but changes nothing, as in Rust and Go, because each case already starts with new objects.

The C++ test program contains the Yon runtime with a test host whose clock stands at 0, every model and entity, every server Setup, and every service, delegate, converter, store, HTTP client, controller and error handler. Caching and stores use the adapters of each class's Setup, as in a running server, and the in-memory entities start empty in each case. `ty test` compiles it with clang++, like a C++ controller, and runs it once; Emscripten is not needed. Calls to the public methods of C++ services, delegates and controllers are recorded, so `ty test --coverage` and the `ty preview` check count real calls.
